lines.text: our relations are exposed at the front? How could we accept
this relative ease if we had not inwardly the readiness to
accept bravely whatever griefs come our way? And if sorrow
came and found us unprepared, could we appropriately say
like Job: "Shall we receive good at the hand of God and
shall we not receive evil?" (Job 2: I0.)
But who is the man who can willingly and trustfully
accept and open his heart to whatever may come to him?
It is the man who can wholly surrender himself to God as
His Creator, and resign himself to God's dealings; who can
sincerely repeat the prayer of our Lord in Gethsemane: "Not
as I will but as Thou wilt" (Matt. 26: 39). It is the man who
knows himself to be the slave of God his Master. It is the
man whom Jesus is referring to in this parable. In another
parable the poet C. F. Meyer expresses the same attitude in
the words which he puts into the mouth of Michaelangelo:
"I who am a slave of passion, make me in Thy image pure
and free! The first man Thou madest out of clay, I will
indeed be made of sterner stuff; forsooth, Master, now Thou
needest Thy hammer! Strike, divine Sculptor, I am the stone."
Because the parable of Jesus invites us to surrender our-
selves in this way, it is a word of grace, a word of liberation.
Because it relentlessly smites from our hands our cherished
rights and claims, it frees us to receive the grace of God. In
the last analysis it has the same meaning as the word:
"Truly I say to you, whoever does not receive the kingdom
of God like a child, shall not enter it" (Mark. Io: 15). To be
God's slave and to be His child is the same thing, and to
those who have the child-like spirit, the promise runs:
"To such belongs the kingdom of God" (v. 14).
But it is not easy to surrender our claimfulness! Is it not
asking too much of our powers? Now the message of Jesus is
finally shown to be a message of grace inasmuch as it drives
us to our last place of refuge, to prayer, in order that we
might receive strength to do what is required. "Rogate!"
